summary: Count the contiguous subarrays whose product is strictly less than k (positive integers).
mainInsight: With positive numbers the product grows when extending right and shrinks when removing from the left, so for each right end shrink l until the product is < k; every start between l and r then gives a valid subarray, adding r - l + 1.

approaches.name: Prefix logs + binary search
approaches.summary: Take logs, use prefix sums and binary search.

approaches.name: Sliding window
approaches.summary: Maintain the product; shrink while >= k; add the window size.

personalSolution.notes: Right approach. Replace `product /= nums[l]` with `//=` to avoid float precision problems.

promptVariants: Which technique counts subarrays with product < k in O(n)?
Why does a sliding window apply?
options: Sliding window (all numbers positive => monotone product)
cards.answer: Sliding window (all numbers positive => monotone product)
cards.explanation: Positivity makes the product monotone in both window ends.

incorrectOptionExplanations.Binary search on the array: Subarray products are not searched in a sorted array.
incorrectOptionExplanations.Hash map of prefix products: Used for exact products, not thresholds.

promptVariants: Why do we add r - l + 1 for each right end?
Explain how counting works per right endpoint.
cards.answer: If the window [l, r] has product < k then every subarray ending at r that starts at any index in [l, r] also has product < k (products of fewer positive numbers are not larger). There are r - l + 1 of them, and each subarray is counted exactly once at its right end.
keyPoints: All suffixes of the window qualify
r - l + 1 subarrays per right end
cards.explanation: The classic 'count subarrays ending at r' trick.

promptVariants: Subarray Product Less Than K runs in ___ time.

cards.explanation: Two pointers and a product variable.

promptVariants: Your code uses `product /= nums[l]`. What is the issue with `/` here and what should you use?
Why is the `l <= r` guard needed when k <= 1?
cards.code:
product = 1
for r in range(n):
    product *= nums[r]
    while product >= k and l <= r:
        product /= nums[l]
        l += 1
    ans += r - l + 1
cards.answer: `/` is true division and produces a float, so for large products precision is lost and the comparison with k can be wrong. Use integer floor division `//=` (exact, because nums[l] divides the product). The `l <= r` guard prevents l passing r when even a single element is >= k (e.g. k <= 1), leaving an empty window with product 1.
cards.explanation: With k <= 1 return 0 up front to avoid the edge case.

promptVariants: What is the answer when k <= 1 (all numbers >= 1)?
cards.explanation: Every product is at least 1, so none is strictly below k <= 1; the window empties and r - l + 1 is 0 each time.
